It also confirms the dataset size: 'We used an adaptation of Plenoxels [14] to collect the dataset of a total of one million SRFs'. The claim accurately reflects the evidence provided in the text.

A Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) is a voxel-based representation of a continuous radiance field where only non-empty voxels are stored, enabling efficient optimization and rendering compared to dense grid methods [S1].

The claim states that SRF is a voxel-based representation where only non-empty voxels are stored, enabling efficient optimization and rendering compared to dense grid methods. Source [S1] explicitly defines SRF as a 'voxel grid' (Section 3.3) and notes that 'Since the SRF is sparse, it can be represented with the COO format... as a set of M tuples' (implying only non-empty voxels are stored). Furthermore, Section 3.3 states, 'The SRF can be viewed as a encoding of the NeRF MLP into sparse voxels for efficient optimization and volume rendering.' The claim accurately reflects these points found in the evidence.
supported

It sets itself apart from dense NeRFs by replacing the implicit MLP with an explicit, sparse 3D grid structure, and from other sparse methods like KiloNeRF by utilizing a direct COO (Coordinate) format storage for irregular volumetric data without hierarchical tree structures [S1, Parent].

The evidence explicitly states that the Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) is a 'voxel grid' (an explicit structure) as opposed to the implicit MLP used in dense NeRFs. It further confirms that the SRF is represented in 'COO format' (Coordinate format) as a set of tuples, which corresponds to the 'direct COO format storage' mentioned in the claim. The evidence describes this as an 'irregular volumetric representation' and does not mention any hierarchical tree structures (like octrees) being used for storage, thereby supporting the distinction from methods using such structures.
